lessons.title: Plains and Their Features
lessons.notes_html:
What a Plain Is

A plain is a broad area of relatively flat land.

Plains are one of the major landforms of the Earth and cover more than one-third of the world's land area.

They exist on every continent.

Physical Features of Plains

Plains are broad, flat or gently rolling areas of low relief with few hills.

Their soil is usually deep and fertile, especially where rivers have deposited alluvium, so they suit farming.

Many plains are grasslands, and the Indus Plain and the Great Plains are large examples given in the chapter.

Major Types of Plains

Alluvial plains are built by river deposits, and flood plains by repeated river flooding.

Coastal plains lie along sea coasts, and lacustrine plains form in former lake basins, like the Kashmir Valley.

Erosional plains are worn flat by rivers, glaciers and wind, while the frozen Arctic plains are called tundra.

lessons.title: Plains, Plateaus, Mountains and Valleys
lessons.notes_html:
What Plateaus Are

A plateau is an area of high, flat land that rises sharply above the surrounding land.

It has a flat top and steep sides, and stands higher than a plain but lower and flatter than a mountain range.

What a Valley Is

A valley is a low area of land between hills or mountains, often with a river flowing through it.

Valleys are usually formed by the erosion of rivers or glaciers cutting down through higher land.

Plains Compared with Other Landforms

Plains are low, flat and broad, while plateaus are high flat-topped areas raised above the surrounding land.

Mountains are the highest landforms, steep and rugged, whereas a valley is a low depression between hills or mountains.

In short: plains are low and flat, plateaus are high and flat, mountains are high and steep, and valleys are low and enclosed.

lessons.title: The River System
lessons.notes_html:
How a River System Works

A river system is a main river together with all its tributaries and the land they drain.

In the upper course the river erodes steep valleys; in the middle course it meanders and deposits silt on flood plains.

In the lower course it deposits its load and forms a delta, and the whole system carries water and sediment to the sea.

What a River System Is

A river system is a main river together with all its tributaries and the area they drain.

Small streams join to form larger tributaries, and all of them flow into the main river.

The whole system drains one basin, carrying water and sediment from the surrounding land to the sea or a lake.

Features Formed by a River

In its upper course a river erodes steep valleys and gorges; in the middle course it forms meanders and flood plains.

Repeated flooding builds levees along its banks, and cut-off meanders become ox-bow lakes.

In the lower course the river deposits its load and forms a delta where it meets the sea or a lake.

lessons.title: The Middle and Lower Course of a River
lessons.notes_html:
Features of the Middle Course

The three main features of the middle course of a river are meanders, flood plains and ox-bow lakes.

In the middle course the river flows more slowly over gentler land, bends into wide curves (meanders), and deposits silt.

When a meander neck is cut off, the abandoned bend remains as an ox-bow lake beside the river.

How a Flood Plain Is Formed

A flood plain is formed when a river floods its banks again and again over a long period of time.

Each flood leaves behind a layer of fine silt and alluvium on the flat land beside the river.

These repeated deposits build up a wide, flat and very fertile plain.

Middle Course Compared with Lower Course

In the middle course the land is gentler, the river flows more slowly, meanders widely and begins depositing silt.

In the lower course the land is almost flat, the river is wide and slow, and deposition dominates over erosion.

The middle course forms meanders, flood plains and ox-bow lakes, while the lower course forms levees and deltas.

lessons.title: Life on the Plains
lessons.notes_html:
The Arctic Plain: A Barren Plain

The Arctic Plain is called a barren plain because its ground stays frozen for most of the year, so trees and tall plants cannot grow there.

The word Tundra itself comes from the Finnish word “tunturi”, meaning a treeless plain, and the chapter describes Arctic plains as frozen, treeless land.

With almost no trees, very little plant growth and long, cold winters, the land looks bare and empty, which is why it is called barren.

Living Conditions in Deserts and the Tundra

Life in a desert or in the Arctic Tundra Plain is hard because of extreme weather and very little water or plant growth.

In a desert, days are very hot and dry, rain is scarce, and only plants and animals that can survive with little water live there.

In the Arctic Tundra, the ground is frozen, trees cannot grow, and people and animals must bear long, bitterly cold winters with only short, cool summers.

In both places people depend on special clothing, shelter and food storage, and they keep animals suited to the climate, such as camels in deserts and reindeer in the far north.

Collecting Pictures of Plains

Use a river plain (for example the Indus Plain), a grassland plain (steppes), a coastal plain and the frozen tundra plain.

Under each picture write one line saying how that plain was formed and where it is found.

lessons.title: Importance of Rivers and Plains
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of Rivers in the Economy

Rivers irrigate crops, supply drinking water and support fishing, which sustain farming and food production.

They provide cheap transport, generate hydropower and recharge groundwater used by towns and farms.

River plains attract settlement, industry and tourism, so rivers raise incomes, trade and the overall economy.

Relief of Pakistan

Pakistan's relief varies from the high Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush mountains in the north to the Potohar Plateau.

Below them lies the vast, flat Indus Plain, while Balochistan has its own plateau and dry mountains.

In the east and south-east are deserts, and in the south the Indus delta meets the Arabian Sea coast.

Why River Plains Are Thickly Populated

River plains are thickly populated because their flat, fertile soil gives rich harvests and water is easily available.

Flat land makes building houses, roads and towns easy, and rivers provide transport, fishing and trade.

Jobs in farming, markets and industry therefore gather people on river plains.

Two Factors That Can Change a River

The two main factors that change a river are erosion and deposition, which alter its course, depth and shape.

Human actions also change rivers: dams store water, embankments control floods, and irrigation canals divert flow.

Together, natural processes and human works can shift a river's channel and change the land around it.

How Dams Affect a River

A dam stores river water, reducing flow downstream and trapping silt that once fertilised flood plains.

This changes habitats for fish and wildlife and can lower water for downstream farms and wetlands.

At the same time dams supply irrigation water, hydropower and flood control, so their effects are both useful and harmful.

Why Deltas Attract People

Deltas attract people because the river deposits rich, fertile silt that suits intensive farming.

Fishing, ports and trade grow at deltas, giving jobs and easy transport by water.

Flat land, water and markets together make deltas busy and densely settled places.

Major Sources of Water on Earth and in Pakistan

On Earth the major sources are oceans, glaciers, lakes, rivers, rain and groundwater stored in aquifers.

Oceans are the largest source, while glaciers store most of the world's fresh water as ice.

What Aquifers Are

Aquifers are underground layers of rock, sand or gravel that hold groundwater.

Water collects in their pores and cracks below the surface of the Earth.

lessons.title: The Water Cycle and Rainfall
lessons.notes_html:
The Water Cycle

Draw the water cycle as a circle: evaporation from seas, lakes and land, then condensation into clouds.

Label precipitation (rain, snow, hail), run-off over the ground, infiltration into the soil, and transpiration from plants.

Mark the four spheres it links: atmosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere.

The Process of the Water Cycle

The Sun's heat evaporates water from oceans, lakes and land, and plants add water by transpiration.

Water vapour cools and condenses into clouds, then falls back as precipitation over land and sea.

Part of it flows in rivers, part sinks into aquifers, and the cycle repeats, constantly renewing the Earth's fresh water supply.

Types of Precipitation

Precipitation is water falling from clouds in liquid or solid form.

Rain is liquid drops; drizzle is fine, light rain; snow is soft ice crystals falling in cold weather.

Sleet is partly frozen rain, and hail is hard balls of ice formed in strong thunderstorm clouds.

What Orographic Rainfall Is

Orographic rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier.

As the air rises it cools, water vapour condenses into clouds, and rain falls on the windward side of the mountain.

The far side, in the rain shadow, receives much less rain.

Measuring Rain

Rain is measured with a rain gauge.

A rain gauge is an open container that collects rainfall, and the depth of collected water shows how much rain fell.

It is usually read in millimetres over a fixed period, such as a day.

lessons.title: Water Purification
lessons.notes_html:
Chlorination

Chlorination is the method of purifying water by adding chlorine, usually as chlorine tablets, to kill germs.

The chapter notes that chlorine tablets should be applied in heated water.

It makes water safe to drink by destroying disease-causing microbes.

Organising Water Purification Methods

Flow chart of the four water purification methods in the chapter: Boiling, then Filtration, then Chlorination, then Reverse Osmosis.

Boiling: heat water to a rolling boil for 1-3 minutes to kill germs and parasites.

Filtration: pass water through chemical and physical filters to remove sediment and chlorine.

Chlorination: add chlorine tablets to heated water to kill germs; Reverse Osmosis: force water through a fine membrane that removes dissolved impurities.

Scarcity of Drinking Water in Cities

Cities face drinking-water scarcity because their growing population raises demand faster than supply.

Leaking pipes, wastage and poor management lose much water before it reaches homes.

Pollution of rivers and falling groundwater levels further reduce the clean water available to cities.

Ways of Using Wastewater

Treated sewage and grey water can be used for watering crops, parks and gardens, and for industry.

It can also recharge groundwater and clean streets, which saves fresh water for drinking.

Wastewater must be treated first: untreated sewage spreads disease, so it is never used directly for drinking.

Uses of Sewage Waste

Treated sewage waste is used to produce biogas, a renewable fuel for cooking, heating and electricity.

Its sludge, after treatment, can be used as manure that adds nutrients to farm soil.

Treated wastewater can also be reused for irrigation and industrial purposes, saving fresh water.

Biogas as a Source of Energy

Biogas is a renewable fuel produced by breaking down organic matter such as food scraps and animal waste without oxygen.

It can be used for cooking, heating, electricity generation and, upgraded to biomethane, as vehicle fuel.

It is a greener fuel because it replaces fossil fuels and uses waste that would otherwise pollute.

Uses of Biogas

Biogas is used as a cooking and heating fuel in homes, replacing wood and fossil fuels.

It is also used to generate electricity and as a vehicle fuel after upgrading to biomethane.

lessons.title: Saving and Managing Water
lessons.notes_html:
Solving the Shortage of Water in Pakistan

Store more water by building dams and small reservoirs, and repair leaking pipes so less water is wasted.

Use water wisely in farming with drip irrigation and lined canals, and harvest rainwater in homes and schools.

Treat and reuse wastewater for irrigation, and teach people to save water instead of wasting it.

If There Is No Water Cycle

Without the water cycle there would be no rain to refill rivers, lakes and aquifers.

Fresh water supplies would run out, crops would fail, and plants, animals and people would face severe drought.

Life on Earth depends on the cycle constantly moving water between sea, sky and land.

Can Biogas Reduce Climate Change?

Yes, biogas can reduce climate change because it replaces coal, oil and gas, cutting carbon dioxide emissions.

It also captures methane from rotting waste, a powerful greenhouse gas, and burns it as useful fuel.

Using waste for energy therefore lowers both fossil-fuel use and uncontrolled methane release.

How Sewage Affects Water Quality

Untreated sewage adds germs, chemicals and nutrients to rivers and lakes, making water unsafe to drink.

Excess nutrients cause algal growth that uses up oxygen, so fish and other aquatic life suffocate and die.

Sewage pollution also spreads disease and damages the whole river ecosystem.

Regions with the Highest Precipitation

The highest precipitation falls in equatorial regions and on windward mountain slopes and monsoon coasts.

Near the equator, warm moist air rises strongly, cools and condenses into heavy rain all year.

Where moist winds are forced up mountains, orographic rain adds further heavy rainfall.

lessons.title: What a Settlement Is
lessons.notes_html:
Meaning of Settlement

A settlement is a place where people live and build homes and other buildings.

It ranges from a tiny hamlet of a few houses to a village, town or large city.

Settlements provide shelter, work, services and community life for their people.

Types of Settlements

Rural settlements include hamlets, with just a few houses, and villages, which may also have a school, shops and a post office.

Urban settlements include towns, larger than villages with secondary schools and markets, and cities, the largest type with hospitals, universities and offices.

Beyond cities are metropolises, conurbations of merged towns, and megalopolises of linked metropolitan regions.

Two Major Types of Settlements Compared

Rural settlements are small, with farming as the main work, open surroundings and few services.

Urban settlements are large and crowded, with jobs in industry, trade and services, and many facilities.

Rural life is quieter and closer to nature, while urban life offers more jobs and services but also pollution and crowding.

Functions of a Settlement

Settlements provide homes and shelter, and they serve as centres for work, trade and transport.

They provide services such as schools, hospitals, markets, banks and government offices.

They also serve cultural, religious and recreational functions, bringing people together for community life.

Administrative Centres

An administrative centre is a town or city where government offices are located.

It is where officials manage the surrounding area, keep records and provide public services.

Examples include district headquarters and provincial capitals.

Route Centres

A route centre is a settlement where several roads, railways or other routes meet.

Because travellers and goods pass through it, markets, workshops and services grow there.

Its importance comes from its position on transport routes rather than from farming.

Activities in an Industrial Town

In an industrial town factories manufacture goods, workshops repair machinery, and warehouses store products.

Workers are employed in production, packaging, transport and trade of manufactured items.

Markets, banks and transport services support the industries located there.

How Towns Differ from Cities

Towns are smaller than cities, with fewer houses, smaller markets and fewer services.

A town may have primary and secondary schools and a railway station, but a city has hospitals, universities, large offices and many industries.

Cities hold far more people and buildings, and offer a much wider range of jobs and facilities than towns.

Conurbations and Megalopolis

A conurbation is a region formed when a number of towns and cities grow and merge into one continuous urban area.

A megalopolis is even larger: a chain of conurbations and metropolises linked together along a corridor.

In short, a conurbation joins neighbouring towns, while a megalopolis joins whole metropolitan regions.

Settlements in Pakistan

Pakistan has rural settlements: hamlets of a few houses and villages with schools, shops and post offices.

Its urban settlements include market towns, industrial towns, ports and large cities such as Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad and Islamabad.

The 2017 census found about 63% of Pakistanis rural and 37% urban, showing both types remain important.

Conditions Suitable for a Settlement

A suitable site has a reliable water supply, flat and fertile land, and a healthy climate.

It needs safety from floods and attacks, building materials, and good transport links by road or river.

Nearby resources, farmland and opportunities for work and trade also help a settlement grow and survive.

How a Settlement Pattern Shapes Lifestyle

In a nucleated settlement houses stand close together, so people share schools, markets and services and live a close community life.

In a dispersed settlement houses stand far apart, so families depend more on their own farms and travel further for services.

In a linear settlement along a road or river, trade and transport shape daily life, while a planned grid settlement gives orderly streets and services.

Land Running Out as Settlements Grow

If towns and cities keep spreading at the present pace, houses, roads and factories will cover more and more open land.

Farmland, forests and natural habitats will shrink, leaving less land for growing food and for wildlife.

To avoid this, growth must be planned: build upwards in cities, protect farmland, and reuse land already built on.

Advantages of rural settlement are clean air, open natural surroundings, close community ties and a lower cost of living.

Rural people may therefore migrate to towns for education, work and better services.

Advantages of urban settlement are many jobs, good schools, hospitals, markets, transport and entertainment.

Urban people enjoy more opportunities but face a busier, more expensive and more polluted life.

lessons.title: How Settlements Change

How Lifestyles Changed with Settlements

Settled life replaced wandering, as people began farming, storing food and living in permanent villages.

Villages grew into towns and cities with markets, schools, hospitals and different jobs beyond farming.

Lifestyles changed from self-sufficient farming to specialised work, trade and urban services.

How Settlements Change over Time

Settlements grow as population rises: hamlets become villages, villages become towns, and towns merge into cities.

New roads, railways, industries and services attract more people and expand the built-up area.

Over time neighbouring towns may join into conurbations, changing land use from fields to housing and industry.

Making Settlements More Sustainable

Settlements become sustainable with planned housing, clean water supply and proper waste disposal and recycling.

Public transport, parks and green spaces reduce pollution and keep the environment healthy.

Saving energy and water, and protecting farmland around towns, keeps settlements livable for future generations.

Problems Cities May Face in Future

Cities may face overcrowding, traffic congestion, housing shortages and rising pollution in future.

Water scarcity, waste disposal and flooding or heatwaves from climate change threaten health and infrastructure.

Unplanned growth may also create slums and strain schools, hospitals and jobs.

Meaning of Agriculture

Agriculture is the cultivation of crops and the farming of cattle, also called husbandry.

It includes growing food crops, keeping animals, fishing and related farm work.

Most of the world's population depends on agriculture directly or indirectly for food and raw materials.

Types of Agriculture

Subsistence agriculture is self-sufficiency farming, where farmers grow enough food crops to feed themselves and their families.

In intensive agriculture, crop growing and cattle breeding are done simultaneously on limited land.

In commercial agriculture, crops are produced on a large scale to earn profit, while traditional farming uses old methods practised for centuries.

Methods of Farming Compared

Subsistence farming grows food mainly for the farmer's own family on small fields, while commercial farming grows crops on a large scale for profit.

Intensive farming gets a large output from a small area with fertilisers and irrigation, while extensive farming uses vast land with machinery.

Traditional methods use old tools and animals, while modern methods use machines, better seeds and scientific techniques.

Important Crops of Pakistan

The important crops of Pakistan are wheat, rice, cotton, sugarcane and maize.

Wheat and rice are staple foods, cotton supplies the textile industry, and sugarcane supplies sugar.

Maize is used for food and fodder, and vegetables such as potato, tomato and onion are also widely grown.

Cash Crops and Staple Crops

Cash crops are grown to sell for profit and as industrial raw material, for example cotton, sugarcane, tobacco and rice.

Staple crops are grown mainly as food for people, for example wheat, maize, millet and gram.

In short: cash crops earn money and feed industry, while staple crops feed the population directly.

Intercropping and Mixed Cropping

Intercropping, or mixed cropping, means sowing more than two crops at the same time in the same field.

Different crops share the land, water and sunlight, and the mixture can reduce pests and improve soil use.

It differs from crop rotation, where crops are grown one after another in different seasons.

Uses of Cotton

Cotton is the main raw material of the textile industry, spun into yarn and woven into cloth.

Its seeds yield cottonseed oil for cooking, and the leftover seed cake is used as animal feed.

Cotton therefore supports farming, industry, exports and millions of jobs in Pakistan.

Raw Materials Obtained from Farming

Farm raw materials such as cotton, sugarcane and wheat feed textile, sugar and flour industries that sell goods at home and abroad.

lessons.title: Challenges Facing Agriculture
lessons.notes_html:
Factors That Affect Agricultural Yield

Yield depends on water supply, soil fertility, quality seed, fertiliser and control of pests and diseases.

Weather matters too: drought, floods, frost and untimely rain can ruin a crop, while good rain and sunshine raise yield.

Modern machinery, credit, storage and fair market prices also affect how much a farmer can produce and earn.

Challenges of Livestock Farming in Pakistan

Livestock farmers face shortage of fodder and clean water, especially in dry seasons, and animal diseases that spread quickly.

Veterinary care, vaccination and good shelters are often lacking, and small farmers get low prices from middlemen.

Heat, floods and poor transport add to the losses, so better feed, health care and markets are needed.

Impacts of Livestock Farming on the Environment

Cattle farming releases methane, a greenhouse gas, from animals and their waste, adding to climate change.

Overgrazing damages grasslands and soil, while animal waste can pollute water if not managed.

Large herds also need much fodder and water, putting pressure on land and water resources.

The Most Challenging Issue in Agriculture Today

The most challenging issue facing agriculture today is water shortage, worsened by climate change.

Changing rainfall, hotter summers and shrinking river flows reduce irrigation water for crops.

Small landholdings, costly inputs and low productivity add to farmers' difficulties.

lessons.title: Improving Agriculture
lessons.notes_html:
Agriculture in the Future

In future more farming will use machines, better seeds, drip irrigation and weather information from mobile phones.

Farmers will grow more high-value crops, fruits and vegetables, and more produce will be processed and packed before sale.

Small scattered fields may join into larger, planned farms, and fewer people will work the land while output per worker rises.

Impact of Agriculture on the Environment

Agriculture feeds people and supplies raw material, but it also affects the environment in harmful ways.

Too much irrigation can cause waterlogging and salinity, chemical fertilisers and pesticides pollute soil and water, and clearing land removes forests.

Livestock adds methane gas, yet careful farming — crop rotation, organic manure and saving water — reduces these harms.

Organic Farming and Its Importance

Organic farming grows crops without chemical fertilisers and pesticides, using natural manure and biological pest control.

It is important because it protects soil health, keeps water and food free from chemical residues, and supports biodiversity.

It gives consumers healthier food and farmers a premium market, though yields may be lower.

Health Risks of GMO Foods

Concerns raised about GMO foods include possible allergic reactions to new proteins in modified crops.

Some people worry about antibiotic-resistance genes and unknown long-term effects on health.

These risks are debated among scientists, so labelling and safety testing of GMO foods are demanded.

Importance of Agriculture for Pakistan

Agriculture is vital for Pakistan's economy: it provides food for the whole population and raw material for textile and other industries.

About 37.4% of the labour force works directly in agriculture and about 70% of the people are linked to it directly or indirectly.

It contributes about one-fifth of GDP, earns foreign exchange through exports like cotton and rice, and supports rural incomes.

Ways to Improve Agriculture in Pakistan

Give farmers better seed, balanced fertiliser and training in modern methods, and improve irrigation so less water is wasted.

Provide easy credit, crop insurance, cold storage and roads to markets so produce is not wasted and farmers get fair prices.

Support research, weather warnings and livestock health services, and teach farmers to protect soil and water.

Climate and Weather Compared

Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere — temperature, rain and wind on a particular day.

Climate is the long-term average pattern of weather in a region, usually over about thirty years.

Weather changes daily, while climate changes only slowly over decades.

Identifying Areas of Climatic Change

Compare temperature and rainfall charts for the same place over many years to spot warming, drying or heavier rain.

In Pakistan this points to the northern glacier areas, the flood-prone Indus Plain and the drought-hit southern regions.

lessons.title: Global Warming and the Greenhouse Effect
lessons.notes_html:
What Global Warming Is

Global warming is the gradual rise in the Earth's average temperature.

It is caused mainly by greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels, which trap extra heat in the atmosphere.

It leads to melting glaciers, rising seas and more extreme weather.

The Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth when greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

Sunlight warms the Earth's surface, which radiates heat upward, and greenhouse gases absorb part of that heat.

This trapped heat keeps the Earth warm enough for life, but extra gases strengthen the effect and cause warming.

The Gas That Absorbs Heat from the Earth

Carbon dioxide is the main gas that absorbs heat radiated from the Earth's surface.

Other greenhouse gases such as methane and water vapour also absorb outgoing heat.

By absorbing this heat, they warm the atmosphere instead of letting it escape to space.

Changes Caused by the Greenhouse Effect

A stronger greenhouse effect raises global temperatures and melts ice caps and glaciers.

Sea levels rise as ice melts and warm water expands, threatening coastal cities and deltas.

Rainfall patterns shift, growing seasons change, and extreme weather such as heatwaves, floods and droughts increases.

Importance of the Ozone Layer

Yes, the ozone layer is very important because it acts as a shield against the Sun's ultraviolet rays.

It absorbs most UV radiation, protecting human health, crops, animals and marine life.

If the ozone layer thins, skin cancer, eye damage and harm to plants and plankton all increase.

Benefits of Ozone Gas

Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays before they reach Earth.

Why We Care about Ozone Depletion

We care about ozone depletion because a thinner ozone layer lets more harmful ultraviolet rays reach Earth.

Extra UV radiation increases skin cancer and eye cataracts, damages crops, and harms plankton that support ocean food chains.

Protecting ozone therefore protects human health, farming and the whole environment.

lessons.title: Effects of Climate Change
lessons.notes_html:
How Human Activity Causes Climate Change

Burning coal, oil and gas for power, transport and industry releases carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas.

Cutting forests removes trees that absorb carbon dioxide, while farming, livestock and waste add methane and other gases.

These gases trap heat near the Earth, so the atmosphere warms and the climate changes.

Effects of Global Warming on Polar Regions

Warming melts sea ice, glaciers and ice sheets in the Arctic and Antarctic, and the meltwater raises sea levels.

Polar animals such as polar bears and seals lose their ice habitat and food, and thawing permafrost releases more greenhouse gases.

Less white ice also means less sunlight is reflected, so the poles warm even faster.

Effects on People, Lifestyle and Economy

Heatwaves, floods and droughts damage homes, harm health and force people to move from affected areas.

Crops fail, water becomes scarce and food prices rise, changing how families live and work.

Repairing flood damage, losing harvests and paying for health care cost the economy heavily, especially in poor countries.

Analysing the Effects of Climate Change on the Earth

Climate change raises average temperatures, melts glaciers and ice caps, and raises sea levels, flooding coastal areas.

It makes extreme weather more common: heavier floods, longer droughts, stronger storms and more wildfires.

Ecosystems are disturbed as species lose habitats, coral reefs bleach and deserts spread into fertile land.

Effects of Climatic Change on the Earth

Climate change raises average temperatures, melts glaciers and polar ice, and raises sea levels.

It makes rainfall irregular, causing droughts in some regions and floods in others.

Heatwaves, storms and wildfires grow more frequent, harming farming, health, wildlife and coastal settlements.

Climate Change Events in the World

The world has seen record heatwaves, melting Arctic ice and rising sea levels in recent decades.

Severe floods, such as Pakistan's floods in 2022, and hurricanes, droughts and wildfires have become more common.

Shrinking glaciers and shifting rainfall patterns show climate change is already affecting every continent.

Smog in Pakistan: Health and Environmental Effects

Smog harms health: it irritates eyes and throat, worsens asthma and breathing diseases, and is dangerous for children and the elderly.

It cuts visibility, disrupts traffic and flights, damages crops and buildings, and keeps sunlight from reaching the ground.

In Pakistan winter smog in cities like Lahore comes from vehicles, industry, brick kilns and crop burning, and needs cleaner fuel and controls.

lessons.title: Reducing Climate Change
lessons.notes_html:
Ways to Reduce the Greenhouse Effect

Cut greenhouse gases by using solar, wind and hydropower instead of coal, oil and gas, and by saving electricity.

Plant trees, protect forests, use public transport, and follow the 3Rs — reduce, reuse and recycle.

Improve energy efficiency in homes and factories, and reduce waste, so less heat is trapped in the atmosphere.

How We Can Stop the Greenhouse Effect

We can slow the greenhouse effect by burning fewer fossil fuels and using solar, wind and hydropower instead.

Saving electricity, planting trees, using public transport and reducing waste all cut greenhouse gas emissions.

International agreements and cleaner industries are also needed for a lasting solution.

Reducing Plastic Use in Daily Life

Carry cloth bags for shopping, use reusable water bottles, and refuse single-use plastic straws and cutlery.

Choose products with less packaging, reuse plastic containers, and sort plastic waste for recycling.

Small daily choices by many people greatly reduce the plastic reaching landfills and rivers.

Using Renewable Energy

We can use renewable energy by installing solar panels on roofs to make electricity and heat water.

Wind turbines generate electricity from wind, hydropower plants use flowing water, and biogas plants use organic waste.

Renewable energy is clean, never runs out, and reduces pollution and climate change.

The 3Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle

The 3R's are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle — three steps for cutting waste and protecting the environment.

Reduce means using less, for example refusing plastic bags and saving paper and energy.

Reuse means using items again, such as bottles and bags, and Recycle means turning waste material into new products.

lessons.title: Minerals and Mining
lessons.notes_html:
What Minerals Are

Minerals are naturally occurring solid substances found in the Earth, formed by geological processes.

They have a definite composition and are dug out by mining.

Examples from the chapter are coal, salt, gypsum, chromite and iron ore.

Metallic and Non-Metallic Minerals

Metallic minerals contain metals, look shiny, and can be melted and shaped; examples are iron ore and copper.

Non-metallic minerals contain no metals and are usually dull and brittle; examples are salt, gypsum and coal.

Metallic minerals are used for metals and machinery, while non-metallic minerals serve chemical, building and fuel uses.

Types of Mining

The two main types of mining are surface mining and underground mining.

In surface mining, the top layers of soil and rock are removed to expose minerals near the surface.

In underground mining, shafts and tunnels reach deep deposits, and methods such as long-wall mining extract coal along a long face.

Long-Wall and Surface Mining

Long-wall mining (underground): a long coal face is cut by machine, the coal falls onto a conveyor, and the roof is supported as the face advances.

Surface mining (open-pit/strip): the top soil and rock are removed to expose the mineral, which is then dug out in steps or benches.

Factors That Make Gemstone Mining Difficult

Gemstone mines are often in remote, mountainous areas with poor roads, so machinery and workers are hard to bring in.

Mining needs skilled workers, safety equipment and money, which small miners often lack, and unplanned digging wastes precious stones.

Lack of cutting, polishing and marketing facilities means raw stones are sold cheaply instead of earning full value.

Reasons That Hamper Gemstone Yield

Old, unscientific methods break stones and recover only a small part of the deposit, lowering the yield.

There is little geological survey work, so miners dig without knowing where the best deposits lie.

Weak safety rules, shortage of trained workers and poor transport further reduce how much good-quality stone is mined.

Earning More from Gemstone Resources

Cut, polish and set gemstones in Pakistan instead of exporting rough stones, so the value stays in the country.

Train workers in modern mining and gem cutting, and hold exhibitions and online sales to reach world buyers.

Give miners fair prices, proper licences and branding for Pakistani stones like emerald, ruby and topaz.

Uses of Coal

Coal is used for thermal power production, generating electricity in power plants.

It fires brick kilns and cement works, and meets domestic needs for heating and cooking.

Coal is therefore an important, though polluting, fuel for industry and homes in Pakistan.

Coal Usage in Pakistan

In Pakistan coal is used for thermal power production, brick kilns and domestic needs.

It is a cheap fuel, but its use is limited by pollution and by the availability of better fuels.

Coal mining also provides jobs in mining regions, while its smoke and ash harm air quality.

Usefulness of Coal against Its Risks

Coal is useful because it is cheap, abundant and can generate electricity and fire brick kilns.

Its risks include mining accidents, roof collapse, gas explosions, flooding and lung disease from coal dust.

Burning coal also pollutes air and adds greenhouse gases, so its benefits must be weighed against health and environmental costs.

Risk Factors of Coal Mining

Coal miners face roof collapse, gas explosions, flooding and accidents with heavy machinery underground.

Coal dust damages lungs over time, causing breathing diseases among miners.

Mining also harms the environment through land damage, waste heaps and polluted water near mines.

Safety and Health of Coal Miners

Give miners helmets, lamps, masks and strong supports in tunnels, and check roofs and gas levels before every shift.

Provide ventilation, clean drinking water, first aid and regular health check-ups for dust-related lung disease.

Train miners in rescue and safety rules, and make owners follow the law on working hours and compensation.

lessons.title: Mineral Oil, Gas and Industries
lessons.notes_html:
Major Products of Mineral Oil

The major products of mineral oil include gasoline, kerosene oil, wax and coal tar.

Gasoline fuels vehicles, kerosene is used for lighting and cooking, and wax is used in candles and polish.

Other products include diesel, lubricants and raw materials for the chemical industry.

Industries Related to Minerals and Power

Mineral industries include coal mining for thermal power, salt mining at Khewra, and cement works using limestone and gypsum.

Fertiliser plants use gypsum, steel works use iron ore, and oil refineries process mineral oil.

Power industries use coal, gas, oil and hydropower: Ghazi Barotha and Mangla are major hydropower projects.

Fossil Fuels to Generate Power

Fossil fuels are burned to produce heat, which makes steam that drives turbines connected to generators.

Coal fuels thermal power plants, oil runs engines and generators, and natural gas fires efficient power stations.

They give reliable power but release smoke and greenhouse gases, so cleaner alternatives are growing.

Improving the Mining Industry

Survey deposits properly, use modern and safe machinery, and train miners in safe methods.

Build roads and power to mining areas, give miners credit and fair prices, and enforce safety and environmental rules.

Set up processing plants near mines so minerals are refined in Pakistan and create skilled jobs.

lessons.title: Alternative Sources of Energy
lessons.notes_html:
How Wind Electricity Is Generated

Wind-electricity is generated when moving air turns the large blades of a wind turbine.

The spinning blades turn a generator inside the turbine, which converts motion into electricity.

The electricity is then sent through wires to homes, farms and industries.

Alternate Sources of Energy

Solar power uses panels that convert sunlight directly into electricity, with no fuel and no smoke.

Wind power uses turbines whose blades turn generators as wind blows.

Water power, or hydropower, uses dams and flowing rivers: falling water turns turbines, and projects like Ghazi Barotha and Mangla supply cheap electricity.

Importance of Alternative Energy for the Environment

Alternative energy sources give a fuel supply that never runs out and produce zero carbon emissions.

They give clean air and water, no greenhouse gas emissions and no pollution, and a cheaper form of electricity.

They create new jobs and help reverse climate change, making them vital for the environment's future.

Importance of Alternate Sources of Energy

Alternate sources such as solar, wind and hydropower are important because they never run out.

They produce no smoke and no greenhouse gases, giving clean air and water and cheaper electricity over time.

They also create jobs and help reverse climate change, as listed in the chapter's benefits of renewable energy.

Why Solar Energy Is Important for the Future

Solar energy is important for the future because sunlight is free, abundant and never runs out.

It produces electricity without smoke, carbon emissions or fuel imports, and panels work even in remote areas.

As panel costs fall, solar power can meet growing demand while protecting the climate.

Pros and Cons of Wind Energy

Pros of wind energy: it is renewable, clean, produces no emissions, and costs little once turbines are built.

Cons: wind is intermittent, so output varies; turbines need open land, can be noisy, and may affect birds.

Despite these limits, wind power remains a valuable clean source alongside solar and hydropower.

Scarcity of Electricity and Gas in Pakistan

Electricity and gas are scarce in Pakistan because demand has grown faster than new power plants and gas fields.

Dependence on imported fuels, circular debt and old transmission lines add to shortages and load shedding.

Limited investment, losses and rapid urban growth have worsened the gap between supply and demand.

lessons.title: Mining: Challenges and Environment
lessons.notes_html:
Common Challenges of the Mining Industry

The mining industry faces safety dangers such as collapse, explosions and flooding in underground mines.

It faces high costs, falling ore quality as easy deposits run out, and remote, difficult locations.

Environmental rules, water use, waste disposal and price swings in mineral markets add further challenges.

Impacts of Mining on the Environment

Mining removes vegetation and topsoil, damages land and leaves waste heaps and open pits.

It can pollute air with dust and water with chemicals and sediments from mines.

Habitats are destroyed, and abandoned mines may keep leaking pollutants unless the land is restored.
